questions.question_text: Find the gradient of $y=5\arcsin x$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

options.why: Used the $\arccos$ derivative, attaching a minus sign that $\arcsin$ does not carry.
Evaluated $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ but forgot the constant factor $5$.
Dropped the factor $5$ and also used the negative $\arccos$ derivative.

questions.question_text: Find the equation of the tangent to $y=6\arctan x$ at the point where $x=1$.

options.why: Used the correct gradient but took the $y$-intercept to be the $y$-value at $x=1$.
Took the gradient to be $6$, not substituting $x=1$ into $\dfrac{6}{1+x^{2}}$.
Took the gradient to be $6$ and also used the $y$-value at $x=1$ as the intercept.

questions.question_text: Find the $x$-coordinates of the stationary points of $y=x-5\arctan x$.

options.why: Solved $1+x^{2}=5$ as $x^{2}=5$, forgetting to subtract the $1$.
Added $1$ to both sides instead of subtracting it, giving $x^{2}=6$.
Solved $x^{2}=4$ but kept only the positive square root.
Found $\dfrac{d\theta}{dx}$ correctly but never multiplied by the speed $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2$.
Used $\dfrac{d\theta}{dx}=-\dfrac{1}{400+x^{2}}$, omitting the factor $20$ produced by the chain rule.
Omitted the chain-rule factor $20$ and also failed to multiply by the speed $2$.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{d\theta}{dx}=\dfrac{-\frac{20}{x^{2}}}{1+\frac{400}{x^{2}}}=-\dfrac{20}{400+x^{2}}$
At $x=20$: $\dfrac{d\theta}{dx}=-\dfrac{20}{400+400}=-\dfrac{1}{40}$
$\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}=-\dfrac{1}{40}\times 2$
$=-\dfrac{1}{20}$
So $\theta$ is decreasing at $\dfrac{1}{20}$ radians per second.

questions.question_text: Find the exact gradient of the curve $y=x^{2}\arccos x$ at the point where $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

options.why: Dropped the minus sign in the derivative of $\arccos x$, so the second term was added.
Used $\arccos\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, which is the value of $\arcsin\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Evaluated $\arccos\dfrac{1}{2}$ as $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and also lost the minus sign of the $\arccos$ derivative.

questions.solution_text:
$u=x^{2},\quad u'=2x$
$v=\arccos x,\quad v'=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$
$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x\arccos x-\dfrac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$
At $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$: $2x=1$, $\arccos\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $x^{2}=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $\sqrt{1-x^{2}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}$
$=\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$
$=\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$
